item.title: India should scrap equity tax on foreign investors, says Edelweiss chief
item.description: Edelweiss Financial Services Chairman Rashesh Shah said scrapping capital gains tax for FPIs could help revive inflows into Indian equities and support the rupee amid heavy overseas selling ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Divya Patil and Samie Modak India should consider removing the capital gains tax imposed on foreigners to help revive the country’s stock market, Edelweiss Financial Services Ltd. Chairman and Managing Director Rashesh Shah said, adding to a growing clamor for the exemption to boost inflows and support the local currency. “We need to showcase to the foreigners we want them,” Shah said in an interview with Bloomberg Television’s Menaka Doshi and Haslinda Amin in Mumbai on Friday. “If India wants foreign investors to come back, we want India to be a good permanent allocation for foreigners, we should do something and removing capital gains tax for foreigners might be an easier answer.” Shah joins dozens who are pushing the government to exempt foreign portfolio investors from paying long-term capital gains tax on listed equities. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said earlier this week that she will consider tax changes on stocks, but stopped short of confirming whether the government was looking at revisions to capital gains or transaction taxes. Long-term gains on listed equities held for more than a year are taxed at 12.5 per cent, while short-term gains are levied 20 per cent.  Foreign investors have been relentless sellers of Indian stocks, with net outflows exceeding $28 billion so far this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. But a sharp selloff in global artificial-intelligence stocks and a decline in oil prices have prompted some overseas funds to return to the market. Foreign investors have poured in more than $5 billion into Indian equities over the past three weeks, helping drive a nearly 10 per cent rebound in the domestic market, data show. Oil prices and any global risk-off plays are the biggest risks for Indian stocks, Shah said, but added that strong domestic inflows provide support during such times.  Shah estimates that Indian mutual funds could channel about $40 billion to $50 billion annually into equities, while insurance companies and pension funds could contribute another $20 billion to $25 billion. That would translate into new annual domestic equity inflows of roughly $60 billion to $80 billion, he said. A steady supply of domestic capital has created an opportunity for companies to raise more money through initial public offerings, according to Shah. The Edelweiss group is planning an IPO for its asset management business in the next 18 to 24 months, Shah said. Group firm Edelweiss Mutual Fund, which manages assets worth ₹1.8 trillion ($19 billion), counts US private equity firm WestBridge Capital as a key investor. Group firm EAAA India Alternatives began trading this week following an IPO that raised ₹1,200 crore. “We want all our underlying businesses, insurance companies, asset management to eventually IPO and get listed in the market,” he said.

item.title: SpaceX director Donald Harrison resigns from board a day after US election
item.description: Harrison, who joined SpaceX's board in 2015 as part of Google's investment, stepped down on November 4. The exit comes as independent directors of SpaceX and Tesla consider a potential merger ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Carmen Arroyo SpaceX board member Donald Harrison resigned from the role after more than a decade, leaving the company as a group of independent directors consider a potential merger with Tesla Inc. Harrison informed SpaceX of his intention to resign on Nov. 4, one day after the US midterm election, according to a SpaceX filing issued after the close Friday. The company said his decision was not due to any disagreement with the company. Harrison joined the board in 2015 as part of Google’s investment in Musk’s rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company. He was an independent director and still works for Google parent Alphabet Inc., leading its corporate partnerships and development team. SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees of independent directors to consider a potential combination, Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk said last month. There’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of next year so that it closes during this administration, Bloomberg News reported. Musk hasn’t said which board members are on the companies’ special committees. Harrison was among the directors SpaceX considers independent, alongside Ira Ehrenpreis, Roelof Botha, Luke Nosek, Steve Jurvetson and Randy Glein. Alphabet remains one of SpaceX’s leading backers, with the second-biggest shareholding after Musk. The investment weighed on the earnings results Alphabet reported last week due to SpaceX shares declining last quarter. Google and SpaceX have rival AI models and chatbots in Gemini and Grok that compete with Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

item.title: Trump names Stephen Miller as chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
item.description: Trump is reshuffling his White House team days after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, elevating immigration hardliner Stephen Miller ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Jeff Mason and Courtney Subramanian President Donald Trump said he was tapping longtime aide Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff and that Susie Wiles is moving to his political operation, shaking up his White House team days after a devastating midterm result. The move comes after rival Democrats dominated Tuesday’s midterm elections, handily winning control of both chambers of Congress. Elevating Miller, the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration agenda and an advocate of aggressive administrative actions, is a signal the president is unlikely to moderate his policies or seek compromises with the new legislature despite an election that offered a sharp rebuke to his second term. The departure of Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, deprives the president of a trusted adviser who quietly wielded considerable control over the West Wing’s operations as he prepares for a lame-duck period and a hostile Democratic Congress that has vowed to ramp up oversight of the administration and his family’s business dealings. “I wanted to make a change,” Trump said, while leaving the White House on Friday. “Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it. Very good, politically.” More changes could be on the way. Trump, in an interview with CBS’ 60 Minutes taped Friday before the Miller announcement, was asked if he expected to fire anyone following the midterm loss.  “I do, yeah,” Trump said, according to an excerpt released by the network. “I love my cabinet. I think they’re good,” he added, but said there may be a “few changes.” Wiles in a statement said Friday would be her last day as chief of staff. She gave the president her resignation on Thursday night, according to a person familiar with the matter. “Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles said. “More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.” Wiles’ White House exit caps what has been a challenging stretch for the chief of staff. She said in March that she’d been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer but continued to work in her role while undergoing treatment. In September, she announced she was cancer-free. Trump had also been asking allies for their views on Wiles and mulling potential replacements for her, Politico reported in October, citing people with direct knowledge of the conversations. Trump at the time told the outlet he had “COMPLETE confidence” in Wiles and derided Politico’s reporting as “TOTAL FAKE NEWS.” In Miller, currently the deputy White House chief of staff and homeland security adviser, Trump is enlisting one of his closest and most powerful advisers, instrumental in the mass deportation raids of undocumented migrants and the narrowing of legal pathways to migration. Miller, 41, served as a senior policy adviser during the first term, writing speeches for the president including his 2017 inauguration address, in which Trump cast a troubling picture of the state of the nation and vowed to reverse what he called “American carnage.” He was a key player behind some of the most controversial policies during Trump’s first administration, including the travel ban and the practice of separating migrant children from their parents at the US-Mexico border. Following Trump’s 2020 election loss, Miller remained in his inner circle and founded America First Legal, a foundation that mounted challenges to corporate diversity, equality and inclusion efforts. Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, vowed to investigate Miller over his role in the administration’s immigration policies, telling him in a statement to “lawyer up.” “Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down,” Garcia added. ‘Ice Maiden’Wiles, 69, was largely viewed as the power center in Trump’s inner circle, appearing by the president’s side at key moments, including inside the makeshift Situation Room at Mar-a-Lago when the US launched military strikes against Iran in late February. That conflict was a major contributor to Republicans’ poor midterm showing after it brought a spike in energy prices that further squeezed household budgets. Trump, who has referred to Wiles as an “ice maiden,” frequently praised his top aide for her steady leadership on his campaign and in the White House. Wiles previously managed Trump’s 2024 campaign, a role in which she was lauded for largely controlling the infighting and turmoil that plagued the president’s earlier runs.  But Wiles was not without her detractors. Critics questioned Wiles’ hold on the job after it emerged that she was not involved in the decision to hire Katie Zacharia, who was named press secretary but abruptly resigned just days later after an unsteady performance in her initial interactions with the media. Scrutiny also fell on two Trump operatives aligned with Wiles, James Blair and Chris LaCivita, for work they did for the pro-Russian government of Republika Srpska. Wiles’ daughter also worked for a firm paid to represent the Balkan territory. A former White House official, Calley Means, criticised Wiles in a podcast with Joe Rogan that was published Friday afternoon, accusing her of slowing down policies popular with voters and using her perch to enrich her family. Means was a close adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and resigned shortly before the midterm elections amid food policy disagreements. While turnover at the White House is ordinary after midterm elections, it wasn’t clear that Wiles’ departure had been preplanned. The move comes as the White House has a planned gathering for cabinet members and their families over the weekend at Camp David, according to a person familiar. Wiles isn’t scheduled to attend, the person said.  Wiles largely avoided the spotlight during her time in the White House, leaning into her role as a deft political strategist and behind-the-scenes operator.  She raised eyebrows in December, however, when Vanity Fair published a bombshell piece in which she offered candid observations on a range of White House personalities, calling Vice President JD Vance a “conspiracy theorist” and accusing Elon Musk of being an “avowed” ketamine user. Of her own boss, the president, she said he had an “alcoholic’s personality.” The daughter of the late American football player and broadcaster Pat Summerall, Wiles first entered Trump’s orbit in 2015, when she served as his campaign co-chair in her home state of Florida. Two years after Trump’s first successful White House campaign, Wiles helped elect Ron DeSantis to the Florida governor’s mansion. DeSantis is seen as a potential 2028 presidential contender.  She returned to Trump’s team for the 2020 cycle and after his loss to former President Joe Biden served as the CEO of the president’s Save America PAC.

item.title: US offers $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear programme
item.description: State Department's Rewards for Justice programme is offering up to $20 mn and possible relocation for information on Iran's nuclear facilities, equipment and personnel, including nuclear scientists ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US offers $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear programme

US offers $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear programme State Department's Rewards for Justice programme is offering up to $20 mn and possible relocation for information on Iran's nuclear facilities, equipment and personnel, including nuclear scientists

Image Credit: Bloomberg

ANI US 2 min read Last Updated : Nov 07 2026 | 9:39 AM IST

Listen to This Article

The United States military announced on Friday that Washington is offering a $20 million reward "and possible relocation" for details concerning Iran's nuclear programme, even as President Donald Trump asserted that Tehran is eager to conclude the ongoing war. In a post shared on X, the United States Central Command stated that a State Department programme, Rewards for Justice, "is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran's nuclear programme, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community." The initiative was originally founded in 1984 under the national security rewards programme managed by the State Department to provide financial incentives for intelligence that safeguards American lives and interests.

Detailing the rationale behind the announcement, the State Department noted that Tehran's non-compliance with its safeguards obligations to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has resulted in the agency losing "continuity of knowledge" concerning the production and inventory of critical elements such as centrifuges, though the directive outlined no precise parameters regarding what intelligence would secure the full $20 million reward. Meanwhile, President Trump has repeatedly claimed that US forces have successfully dismantled Iran's nuclear programme. Speaking in West Palm Beach, Florida, on Friday evening, the US leader remarked, "If we didn't hit Iran, you wouldn't have Israel today," adding, "If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East."

Despite the military actions, the president pointed out that eight months of conflict have heavily damaged Iran's economy and military, leaving Tehran anxious to make a deal. "We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he stated. Amid these developments, diplomatic efforts involving various mediators have intensified to avert any resumption of fighting. On Tuesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian affirmed that his administration continues to pursue avenues to resolve the crisis through dialogue. Earlier this week, Trump noted that he still needs to address one or two residual sites, specifically mentioning Pickaxe Mountain, located in central Iran, a suspected nuclear facility whose designation has been strongly denied by Tehran.
